attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Dry point etching of the finished Golden Gate Bridge as imagined before it was built. A dramatic low viewpoint from the rocks at the water's edge on the San Francisco side, looking up and out under the south approach: a massive vertical concrete pylon fills the right of the frame, with the steel lattice approach arch springing over the brick casemates of Fort Point beneath it. The south tower stands mid-frame with the main cable sweeping down and away, the deck running off to the left, and the far Marin tower small in the haze at left. Surf breaks over dark rocks along the bottom edge.
details: Construction stage: none — this is a pre-construction artist's conception, published while work was only beginning. It nevertheless predicts the built result closely, including the steel arch that was actually thrown over Fort Point to save the fort. Rendered entirely in fine etched line and crosshatch, with a heavily worked stormy sky. Tall portrait format.
visible_text: None inside the image area; the printed page beneath it is not included in the crop.
notes: By Chesley Bonestell, later famous as a space artist; he worked as an architectural renderer on the Golden Gate Bridge. Useful as an 'what they thought it would look like' cutaway against the reality photographs.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Pen-and-ink drawing printed in dark green ink, portrait format. A single completed bridge tower rises the full height of the frame at left, seen from the water with its stepped portal bracing and X-braced base sitting on a low pier. To the right, Telegraph Hill with Coit Tower on its crown, tiers of San Francisco houses down the slope, and ocean liners and piers along the waterfront at the bottom right. Steeply raked hatching in the sky.
details: Construction stage: none — an imagined finished tower drawn in 1933, the year work started. The tower is drawn free of cables and deck, isolated as a pure vertical object, which makes it read as a monument rather than as part of a bridge. The placement against Telegraph Hill is an artist's conceit, not a real viewpoint.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Commons file description: 'August, 1933: Progress work on the Golden Gate Bridge with late pictures and an original etching by Chesley Bonestell; this drawing by Chesley Bonestell.'

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Soft charcoal or pencil rendering of the completed bridge, wide landscape format. The bridge is seen almost side-on from low over the water: the long suspended span runs from the left edge to a single tower standing on its pier a little right of centre, then the side span and a trestle approach continue right onto a headland. Bluffs and hills recede to the right; a small steamer with a smoke plume sits on the water at left. Large empty grey sky over the top two-thirds of the frame.
details: Construction stage: none — a pre-construction rendering. Drawn in smudged tone rather than line, so the structure reads as a pale silhouette against fog. Note how thin and low the deck is made to look, and how much of the frame is given to empty water and sky.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: One of a group of design-era renderings reproduced in Architect and Engineer in 1933; kept here as pre-construction context for the build sequence.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images), composite by G. Moulin
depicts: Photographic composite: the finished bridge painted or montaged onto a real photograph of the strait, seen from high on the Marin Headlands looking east. The bridge crosses the frame left to right with both towers, main cables, suspenders and deck complete; behind it the whole northern waterfront of San Francisco and the city skyline, with the Presidio and the Marina at right. A ferry steams under the span trailing smoke; bare Marin hillsides fill the bottom of the frame.
details: Construction stage: none — a montage of the proposed bridge onto an existing photograph, made before the structure existed. The give-away is the bridge's flat, drawn quality against the grainy real landscape. The 1930s city behind it is genuine, low-rise and treeless, which makes this useful for establishing what the site looked like at the start.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Commons file description: 'Composite picture of the Golden Gate Bridge by G. Moulin.' Very close in viewpoint to construction-05, which is a sepia calendar version of the same composite.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images), copyright Pacific Portland Cement Company
depicts: Sepia-toned reproduction of the same kind of pre-construction composite: the completed bridge seen from the Marin Headlands looking east across the strait to San Francisco, a ferry steaming beneath it, bare Marin ridgelines in the foreground and a low fog bank over the city.
details: Construction stage: none — a promotional image of the bridge as it would look, issued by a cement supplier while the piers were still being poured. Warm sepia print, softer and grainier than construction-04. The whole northern shore of San Francisco is visible behind the span with almost no tall buildings.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left of the image: 'COPYRIGHT 1933 - BY THE PACIFIC PORTLAND CEMENT COMPANY'.
notes: Commons file description: 'Golden Gate Bridge pictured on Pacific Portland Cement calendar.' Shows how the unbuilt bridge was already being used to sell materials.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Wide panoramic rendering of the whole bridge in elevation, drawn in soft pencil tone. Reading left to right: the trestle-and-truss approach viaduct, the tall arched span carried over Fort Point (drawn as a steel arch springing between two piers with a building beneath it), then a pylon, then the south tower on its pier, and the main span with its cable curve and suspender rods running off to the right where the far tower stands.
details: Construction stage: none — a design elevation of the completed structure. Its value is that it lays out the whole anatomy of the bridge in one strip: approach viaduct, arch over the fort, pylon, tower, main span. Extremely wide aspect ratio (about 2.5:1), so it will need a full-bleed band or a pan rather than a normal 16:9 fill.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Retrieved via a Commons full-text search on 'south tower caisson'; from the same 1933 Architect and Engineer run as the other renderings.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: Ground-level view over the construction site at Fort Point, looking north-west across the strait. In the foreground the cliff has been cut and terraced into raw white rock and spoil; two tall lattice derrick masts stand at left with their guy wires running across the frame. Beyond them a dark brick building and a group of white frame houses on the bluff, and out in the water a long timber trestle running out from the shore with a derrick working at its end. The Marin Headlands make the far horizon.
details: Construction stage: earliest site work, 1933. No tower steel anywhere — only excavation, derricks, and the access trestle being pushed out toward the south pier site. The white frame buildings on the bluff are the Fort Point lighthouse keepers' residences, still standing; they were later demolished for the bridge approach. The ground is torn open and littered with timber and plant.
visible_text: None burned into the image. A printed credit line runs under the photograph: 'Golden Gate NRA, Park Archives, Fort Point Photo Collection - Historic (through 1971), GOGA 35339.098'.
notes: Commons description notes the lighthouse keepers' houses are still intact, which dates the frame to the very start of the job.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: View of Fort Point, the brick coastal fort at the San Francisco anchorage of the strait, with the bridge job going on around it. The fort sits low in the middle distance behind its seawall; construction plant, stacked material and a trestle running out into the water are visible beside it, with the Marin shore across the strait.
details: Construction stage: early 1933. The site is a staging yard — the area around the fort is being used to lay down construction material, and the access trestle is out in the water, but there is no tower steel and no pylon concrete yet.
visible_text: None burned into the image; the source carries an NPS credit line.
notes: Commons description: 'This photo, taken around 1933, shows the early construction phase of the Golden Gate Bridge. Notice that the southeast area of Fort Point was used as a staging area for construction materials.'

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Tall portrait aerial photograph taken from about a thousand feet, looking down and out from the San Francisco shore. The long timber access trestle runs from the bottom of the frame straight out into open water toward the south pier site, with derricks and a work platform at its far end. Shoreline installations, spoil and roads fill the bottom third; open water and the Marin shore fill the top.
details: Construction stage: south pier access work, 1933 — the hardest part of the whole job. This is the trestle that had to be pushed 1,000 ft out into the open ocean to reach the south tower foundation. No pier concrete, no tower steel. Strongly vertical composition looking straight down the line of the trestle.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Commons description: 'Aerial view at 1000 feet elevation, showing access trestle to south pier site on San Francisco side, Golden Gate Bridge. About 800 feet of this trestle was swept away by heavy seas December 13' — i.e. the structure shown here was largely destroyed by a storm in December 1933.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: The Marin-side cable anchorage under construction on a bare grass hillside. A run of enormous stepped concrete blocks climbs the slope from lower left to upper right, several still inside timber formwork with scaffolding and reinforcing steel exposed. A tall lattice derrick mast with a long boom stands at left centre; a dark rock outcrop rises behind the concrete. Uncut grass in the foreground.
details: Construction stage: anchorage construction, 1933 — the concrete mass into which the main cable strands would later be splayed and locked. No cable, no tower steel in frame at all. The blocks are being poured in stepped lifts; the timber formwork and the derrick give the scale.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Commons description: 'Cable anchorage for the Golden Gate Bridge, Marin side.' Small file (950x626) but comfortably over the size floor, and one of very few images of the anchorages under construction.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: A large group of Civilian Conservation Corps men from the Muir Woods camp posed in rows for a group photograph at Fort Baker on the Marin shore. Behind them, across open ground, the Golden Gate Bridge job is under way — heavy concrete anchorage and pylon work and steel rising at the water's edge.
details: Construction stage: Marin-side anchorage and pylon work, mid-1930s. The bridge is background rather than subject, but it gives the north approach at an early stage with concrete blocks in place. Useful for the Depression-era labour context around the project.
visible_text: None burned into the image; NPS credit line printed beneath.
notes: Overlaps with the labor theme, but kept here for the Marin-side structure visible behind the group.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Four men in suits, jackets and lace-up riding boots stand at the base of an enormous freshly poured concrete block, which fills the right two-thirds of the frame in stepped, buttressed faces. Three more men stand on top of the block against the sky, one beside what looks like a surveying instrument; a timber ladder and formwork lean against the left end. Bare graded dirt in the foreground.
details: Construction stage: anchorage / pylon concrete, 1933. The men give the scale precisely — the block is perhaps four or five times their height. The concrete is new and unweathered, with the horizontal lift lines and vertical form marks still crisp. A good image for the sheer volume of the foundations rather than the glamour of the towers.
visible_text: Printed caption below the photograph: '"Golden Gate" Cement used.'
notes: From the 1933 Architect and Engineer feature; the caption is a supplier plug, which is itself a period detail.

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: Two tall concrete pylon shafts stand in the foreground, their tops crowned with dense cages of reinforcing steel and timber formwork; a lattice derrick mast rises between them and guy wires cut diagonally right across the frame. Beyond them, across the water, the steel frame of the Marin tower is going up on its pier and fender, with a stern-wheel-looking work boat alongside and the Lime Point cliff behind. Site buildings and plant crowd the bottom edge.
details: Construction stage: San Francisco-side pylon concrete plus Marin tower steel erection, 1933-34. The Marin tower is still only a stub — roughly the height of its base bracing — while the near pylons are being topped out. Everything is criss-crossed with derrick guy wires, which is a strong graphic feature.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Commons description: 'Golden Gate Bridge, showing location of Pylon G1 with Marin tower erection in the background.'

attribution: Architect and Engineer magazine, 1933 (via Internet Archive Book Images)
depicts: A very high-contrast, hazy photograph looking out across flat water into a low sun. Almost the whole frame is empty silver water and sky; at the right stands the black silhouette of the partly built Marin tower — two vertical legs joined by a portal, with a creeper derrick perched on top — rising from its pier and fender, with a dark headland behind it and a work boat below.
details: Construction stage: Marin (north) tower erection, 1933-34, with only the lower shaft standing. Almost abstract: a single dark vertical against an empty field. Nothing else of the bridge exists in the frame — no cables, no deck, no south tower.
visible_text: No text inside the image area.
notes: Retrieved via Commons full-text search; from the same 1933 Architect and Engineer run.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: U.S. Army Air Corps oblique aerial looking north-east over Lime Point on the Marin shore. The partly built north tower stands on its pier at the foot of a huge crumbling cliff, its lower shaft up and topped with a creeper derrick; the pier apron below it is a raft of timber staging and plant, with a white lighthouse building at the water's edge. Beyond, Horseshoe Bay and Fort Baker, then Angel Island and the Tiburon shore across the bay.
details: Construction stage: Marin tower erection, January 1934 — the tower is up perhaps a third of its final height, still a plain shaft with no portal openings visible above the base. Nothing exists on the San Francisco side of the strait in this frame. The scale of the cliff against the tower is the point of the picture.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left of the print: '1-5-34 GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE'. Typed archival header above the mount: 'AIRSCAPES - California' and 'Orig. neg. rec'd 17 April 1959 from ACRPL-11. Copy neg. made 17 April 1959 and orig. destroyed. (Nitrate Film).' Negative number '161914 A.C.' lower right.
notes: The print is photographed on its archival mount, so a typed border and punch holes surround the image; it can be cropped to the picture area if needed.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial, near-vertical down the line of the north tower. The tower now rises as a tall pale shaft filling the centre of the frame, with a creeper derrick and boom working at its very top and open cell shafts visible in its face. Its base sits on a timber-decked pier crowded with plant, and immediately below it are the white gabled buildings and lighthouse of Lime Point. The Marin cliff throws a black shadow across the left; open water fills the right half.
details: Construction stage: Marin tower erection, March 1934 — two months later than construction-15 and visibly much taller, with the derrick creeping up the shaft as it goes. Still no cables, no catwalks, and nothing built across the strait. The Lime Point lighthouse keeper's house right at the tower's foot gives the domestic scale.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left: '3-4-34 GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE CONSTRUCTION'. Typed archival header: 'AIRSCAPES - California' with the 1959 nitrate copy-negative note.
notes: Same Air Corps series as construction-15; a clean two-month progress pair with it.

attribution: Roger Sturtevant, Historic American Buildings Survey
depicts: Large-format ground photograph looking north-west past Fort Point. The brick fort fills the right half of the frame, its arched casemate windows and pale granite quoins sharp in raking sun. Rising directly behind and above it are the two enormous concrete shafts of the south approach pylon, still under construction — their tops open, wrapped in timber formwork and bristling with reinforcing bars, with a horizontal steel strut between them and a tall derrick mast alongside. A dozen 1930s cars are parked along the fort wall; the ground in front is torn up with excavation and a concrete-lined pit. The steel of the Marin tower shows tiny at the far left across the water.
details: Construction stage: south approach pylons under construction, 31 May 1934. The pylons are perhaps four-fifths poured and topped out with rebar and forms; the Marin tower is standing but the south tower is not visible. This is the classic image of the 1860s fort about to be built over: the surveyors were documenting the fort precisely because the bridge threatened it.
visible_text: Burned into the lower right of the negative: '38-P193-1'.
notes: Shot for the Historic American Buildings Survey. A wider variant of the same negative with a full HABS caption strip also exists on Commons; this is the cleaner crop.

attribution: U.S. Army (via U.S. National Park Service)
depicts: View of the early bridge works rising over Fort Point: the fort's brick mass low in the frame with the tall concrete south approach pylons standing behind it, and construction plant around the base.
details: Construction stage: south approach pylon concrete, 1933-34. The main span does not exist yet in this frame. Shows the same confrontation of nineteenth-century brick fort and twentieth-century concrete as construction-17, from a different distance.
visible_text: None burned into the image.
notes: Commons title: 'Early construction of the Golden Gate Bridge over Fort Point.' Smaller file (1024x813) but well over the floor.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial looking north across the strait. In the foreground at bottom right, the San Francisco shore: Fort Point with its brick walls and, rising immediately beside it, the twin concrete shafts of the south approach pylon, plus derricks, huts and torn ground. From that shore a long straight timber trestle runs out into the water toward the south pier site, where a derrick barge and work platform sit at its far end in a swirl of tide. Across the strait at upper left, the steel frame of the Marin tower stands on its pier at Lime Point. Beyond, the Marin hills, Horseshoe Bay, Angel Island and the bay.
details: Construction stage: June 1934 — the single best frame in the pool for showing the two sides of the job at once. South side: pylons up, trestle out, pier not yet built. North side: tower steel standing. Nothing spans the water between them; the visible tide rips across the middle of the strait make the point about the currents.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left: '6-1-34 GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE CONSTRUCTION'. Negative number 'B 161914 A.C.' lower right. Typed archival header 'AIRSCAPES - California' with the 1959 nitrate note.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial of the San Francisco side of the works: Fort Point and the approach pylons on the bluff, the construction yard behind them, and the access trestle running out from the shore across open water to the south pier site with work craft alongside.
details: Construction stage: south pier work, late June 1934 — three weeks after construction-19 and from a similar vantage. The trestle and pier site are the subject; the deep water and moving tide around the pier site are visible as pale streaks.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip along the lower edge dated 6-26-34, in the same Air Corps format as the rest of this series; typed archival header above the mount.
notes: One of a long run of dated Air Corps progress obliques (NARA 'California - San Francisco' series) that together give a month-by-month build sequence.

attribution: Associated Oil Company / Chas. M. Hiller (Library of Congress)
depicts: High oblique aerial looking north from over the Presidio. The foreground is the whole San Francisco headland — Fort Winfield Scott's barracks and parade grounds, roads, eucalyptus stands and the beach curving right. At the shore edge, the twin white pylon shafts stand beside Fort Point with the long access trestle running out into the strait to a derrick barge. Across the water, the dark steel shaft of the partly built Marin tower rises at Lime Point. Bare Marin ridges fill the top third; a freighter crosses at left.
details: Construction stage: 1934 — pylons poured, trestle out to the south pier site, Marin tower steel up to roughly half height, no south tower, no cables. Gives the whole San Francisco approach landscape in one frame, almost entirely treeless and military.
visible_text: Watermark burned into the lower left: 'ASSOCIATED OIL COMPANY'.

attribution: Associated Oil Company / Chas. M. Hiller (Library of Congress)
depicts: Aerial of the strait with the works on both shores: the south pier and its fender ring out in the water with the first concrete tower bases on it, the access trestle running back to the San Francisco shore, and across the water the steel frame of the Marin tower standing on its pier.
details: Construction stage: 16 July 1934 — the south pier and fender are built and the south tower is only just beginning at its base, while the Marin tower steel is well up. This is the moment the two sides are furthest out of step.
visible_text: Associated Oil Company watermark.
notes: Library of Congress copy, 3c22793u. Same date and photographer as construction-23, which is the portrait framing.

attribution: Associated Oil Company / Chas. M. Hiller (Library of Congress)
depicts: Portrait-format aerial looking along the line of the bridge: the south pier and its elliptical fender wall sit in open water in the lower half of the frame with the access trestle running back to shore, and beyond them the Marin tower's steel frame rises on the far shore.
details: Construction stage: 16 July 1934, same day as construction-22 but framed vertically to stack the south pier below the Marin tower. Tall portrait aspect (1920x2398) — a real constraint for a 16:9 deck; best used cropped or as a full-height panel.
visible_text: Associated Oil Company watermark.
notes: Library of Congress copy, 3c00678u.

attribution: ACME Newspictures
depicts: Press photograph, aerial: the completed steel frame of the north (Marin) tower standing alone on its pier at the water's edge, seen from the air with the Marin shore behind it. The pier apron and fender around its base are stacked with plant, and a contractor's sign board is visible on the works below.
details: Construction stage: north tower steel complete, 9 August 1934. The tower is topped out at its full 746 ft with the portal bracing in place, but there is no cable, no catwalk, and no south tower — it stands entirely by itself. A press photograph, so it was distributed with a typed caption.
visible_text: A contractor's sign board is legible on the works beside the tower base.
notes: ACME caption on the Commons file: 'A new air view of the mighty structure which will support the Golden Gate Bridge at its north terminus on the Marin County shores of San Francisco Bay. Entirely completed, the main tower contains 20,360 tons of structural steel and is 746 feet high.'

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial of the strait with naval vessels standing in through the Golden Gate. The partly built Marin tower stands on its pier at the Marin shore; the ships pass through open water where the bridge will later be.
details: Construction stage: December 1934 — north tower steel standing, south tower not yet up, nothing spanning the water. The ships passing freely through the gap under where the bridge will be is the visual point.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 12-8-34 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: Fort Point seen almost surrounded by the bridge works: the brick fort in the middle of the frame with the concrete approach pylons rising beside and behind it, construction plant and roads cut into the bluff around it, and the tower steel out in the strait beyond.
details: Construction stage: south approach and south tower work, 1934-35. Shows how completely the project enclosed the fort. The lighthouse keepers' residences visible in the earliest frames of this pool are gone or going here.
visible_text: None burned into the image; NPS credit line beneath.
notes: Commons description: 'Notice how Fort Point has been surrounded by the construction project. All of the lighthouse keepers' residences were ultimately demolished to make way for the bridge on-ramp.'

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps aerial with a formation of military aircraft in the foreground and the bridge works below and beyond. The north tower stands complete on the Marin shore; the south tower is up only part way on its pier out in the strait.
details: Construction stage: March 1935 — north tower finished, south tower rising. The two towers at visibly different heights in the same frame is the useful thing here. No cables, no catwalks, no deck.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 3-23-35 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives (Mildred Lewis Collection)
depicts: A wide, low-resolution snapshot across the water: at left the stub of the south tower under construction on its pier, at right the completed steel of the Marin tower on the far shore, with the headlands behind.
details: Construction stage: south tower part-built, north tower complete — so 1935. A private snapshot rather than an official photograph, which gives it a different, plainer look. Small file (1040x662) and soft, but the two towers at different heights read clearly.
visible_text: None burned into the image; NPS credit line beneath.
notes: Commons description: 'Golden Gate Bridge construction. Mildred Lewis Collection.'

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial across the strait. Both towers now stand complete and bare on their piers, the near one out in the water and the far one at the Marin shore, with nothing at all between them. The San Francisco shore and the works run along one edge; the Bay Bridge, also under construction, is visible in the distance behind the city.
details: Construction stage: May 1935 — both towers topped out, no catwalks, no cables, no deck. This is the emptiest and most striking configuration of the whole build: two 746 ft towers standing in the sea with a two-thirds-of-a-mile hole between them. Two enormous bridges under construction in one frame.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 5-3-35 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: A large roadside billboard photographed head-on from the far side of a fence and a strip of grass, with a lattice-work skirt below it and a wooden rail fence in front. The board carries a painted long-section diagram of the whole bridge — approach viaduct, pylons, both towers, cable curve, roadway and the sea bed profile beneath — with dimension callouts, and a row of vertical thermometer gauges standing at each element to show how far each contract had progressed, filled in red.
details: Construction stage: a progress board rather than the structure itself, photographed 5 April 1935. This is the single most text-dense image in the pool and is effectively a data graphic of the project as of March 1935. The thermometers show the contracts at very different levels of completion. The billboard stands in bare grass beside a road with a parked car and a shed visible behind it.
visible_text: Header on the board: 'THE GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE'. On the diagram: 'TOTAL LENGTH 6450 FEET', '4200 FT. SPAN', '1125 FT. SPAN', '750 FT', '250 FT', 'A $35,000,000 PROJECT', 'STARTED 1933', 'COMPLETION 1937', 'Joseph B. Strauss, Chief Engineer', 'SAN FRANCISCO SIDE', 'MARIN COUNTY SIDE', 'SOUTH TOWER PIER & FENDER', 'NORTH TOWER AND PIER', 'ANCHORAGE', 'PYLON', 'APPROACH SPANS', 'PRESIDIO ROADS', 'MARIN COUNTY ROADS', 'THE TOTAL PROJECT PROGRESS SCHEDULE / Percentage Completed Mar 1st 1935 is shown in red', 'Prepared for your information by'. Contractor list: 'MAIN STEEL STRUCTURES - McCLINTIC-MARSHALL CORP.', 'MAIN CABLES - JOHN A. ROEBLING'S SONS', 'MAIN PIERS & FENDER - PACIFIC BRIDGE CO.', 'ANCHORAGES - BARRETT & HILP', 'STEEL APPROACH SPANS - EATON AND SMITH', 'PRESIDIO ROAD - RIMBEY-RAYMOND', 'ELECTRIC WORK - ALTA ELECTRIC & MECHANICAL CO.', plus the 'Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District Directorate' name list (Filmer, Keesling, Lutgens, McLaughlin, Newhouse, Shannon, Brown, Welch, Doyle, McMinn, O'Brien, Trumbull, Maxwell, McVay). Burned-in strip: '(652-32I-15)(4-5-35-11:00A.) GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE DATA.' Typed archival header: 'Rec'd from Crissy Field, Calif. - 5/13/35' and 'Golden Gate Bridge - San Francisco, Calif. to Marin County, Calif.'
notes: Names every prime contractor including John A. Roebling's Sons for the cables, and puts a dollar figure and a completion date on the board while the job was half done.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Wide Air Corps aerial over San Francisco Bay with both of the city's great bridges under construction at once — the Golden Gate Bridge at the mouth of the strait with its two towers standing, and the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge stretching across the bay behind the city.
details: Construction stage: October 1935 — both Golden Gate towers complete, spinning not yet finished; the Bay Bridge is simultaneously under construction. Useful for the 'two bridges at once in the depths of the Depression' point.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 10-14-35 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial of the bridge site with both towers standing complete on their piers and the first lines strung between them across the gap.
details: Construction stage: October 1935 — towers finished and the first ropes and catwalk stringing appearing between the tower tops. There is still no deck and no spun cable; what runs between the towers is a thin line, not the heavy cable curve seen in the 1936 frames.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 10-14-35 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps aerial over Crissy Field and the Presidio shoreline with the bridge works in the distance at the mouth of the strait: both towers standing, lines strung between them, and the Marin Headlands beyond.
details: Construction stage: October 1935. The bridge is small in the frame — the subject is really the Army airfield and shore in the foreground — but the two towers and the strung lines are legible. Good for establishing the setting rather than the structure.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 10-14-35 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial taken from over the Marin Headlands looking across to San Francisco. Both towers stand complete with lines strung between and behind them; the bare Marin ridges fill the foreground.
details: Construction stage: mid-October 1935 — catwalk stringing under way, no spun cable, no deck. The reverse viewpoint to most of the pool, looking from Marin toward the city.
visible_text: Burned-in caption strip dated 10-16-35 in the standard Air Corps format; typed archival header above the mount.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: View across Crissy Field and the Presidio shoreline to the bridge, with both towers standing and the catwalks strung between them.
details: Construction stage: catwalks strung, cables not yet complete, no deck — late 1935 or early 1936. Foregrounds the Army airfield and the shore in front of the works.
visible_text: None burned into the image; NPS credit line beneath.
notes: Commons title: 'Fort Point, the Golden Gate bridge construction, and Crissy Field.'

attribution: U.S. Army (via Wikimedia Commons)
depicts: A four-engined Martin flying boat, white-hulled with a row of round cabin windows, banks across the middle of the frame low over the strait. Behind and to the left stands one completed but bare bridge tower on the Marin shore; to the right, close to the camera, stands the other completed tower on its pier and fender in open water, with a small boat alongside. Marin hills and Angel Island fill the top of the frame.
details: Construction stage: both towers topped out, absolutely nothing between them — no catwalk, no cable, no deck. So 1935, between the completion of the south tower and the start of catwalk stringing. The aircraft is flying through the gap where the roadway would be. A striking 'two towers and a hole' composition with a period aircraft to date it.
visible_text: No text burned into the image.
notes: Commons title: 'Aerial view of plane flying over the Golden Gate Bridge before completion.' The aircraft is a Martin M-130 type flying boat of the kind Pan American flew from Alameda from 1935.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial taken from above Fort Baker on the Marin side, looking south-west down the line of the bridge. The near (north) tower stands complete, pale and open, on its pier in the water at centre; the far (south) tower stands in silhouette across the strait at upper left. Heavy parallel curves sweep from the top of each tower down toward the water and back up — the strung catwalks and their hand-ropes. Along the bottom right the Marin approach works: the huge blank concrete faces of the north anchorage and the twin north pylons, with derricks, huts, a spoil slope and the beach.
details: Construction stage: 28 January 1936, catwalks strung and spinning under way. Both towers complete; the catwalk footbridges hang the full length of the main span in two curves; there is no deck of any kind and nothing but air under the curves. The anchorage and pylon concrete in the foreground is finished and unweathered.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left of the print: '(0-15-32I-HF)(1-28-36-1:00P)(12-1000)  GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE. FORT BAKER CALIF.' Typed archival header: 'San Francisco, Calif. - Golden Gate Bridge' and 'Rec'd from Hamilton Field, Calif. - 2/14/36'.
notes: One of the strongest images in the pool for the catwalk-and-spinning stage.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Two twin-engined Martin B-12 bombers in formation fly left to right across the middle of the frame, seen from above and behind, with the whole of San Francisco spread below them — dense grids of low houses running to the Presidio's green, the Marina, and Crissy Field. Beyond, the strait with the bridge under construction, both towers standing with the cable curves between them, and the Marin Headlands and Mount Tamalpais filling the top of the frame.
details: Construction stage: 28 January 1936, same day as construction-37 — catwalks strung, spinning under way, no deck. The bridge is a small element on the far side of the city, so this works as an establishing shot of 1930s San Francisco with the half-built bridge in it rather than as a structural image. Aircraft serials are painted on the tails.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left: '(0-19-32J-HF)(1-28-36-1:25P.)(12-2000)  BOMBERS OVER SAN FRANCISCO CALIF.' Typed archival header: 'San Francisco, Calif. - Martin B-12 Airplanes over Golden Gate Bridge' and 'Rec'd from Hamilton Field, Calif. - 2/14/36'; handwritten annotations on the mount including '1 print each given Nat. Geo. Society 2/6/36'.

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Air Corps oblique aerial over Crissy Field: the Army airfield's grass runway and hangars run diagonally across the bottom of the frame with long dark files of troops drawn up on the field and crowds lining the edges. Beyond, the beach curves out to Fort Point, and across the water the bridge stands with both towers complete and heavy cable and catwalk curves slung between them and back to the anchorages. The Marin Headlands and the open Pacific fill the top of the frame.
details: Construction stage: 4 April 1936, cable spinning well advanced — the curves between the towers are now thick and dark, not thin lines, and they run down to the anchorages on both shores. Still no deck at all. The military ceremony in the foreground gives an unusual amount of human activity for an aerial.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left: '(0152-32-I-15)(4-4-36-2P)(12-1000)  ARMY DAY ACTIVITIES, CRISSY FIELD, CALIF.' Typed archival header: 'Golden Gate Bridge - San Francisco, Calif.' and 'Rec'd from Crissy Field, Calif. - 5/8/36'.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: Aerial view of the bridge with both towers standing, catwalks strung between them and the main cables being spun, and no roadway of any kind between the towers.
details: Construction stage: cable spinning, 1936. The gap between the towers holds only the catwalk footbridges and the growing cable; there is nothing to walk or drive on.
visible_text: None burned into the image; NPS / Golden Gate NRA credit line beneath.
notes: Commons title: 'The Golden Gate Bridge under construction.'

attribution: U.S. Army Air Corps (U.S. National Archives)
depicts: Large, very sharp Air Corps oblique aerial looking north-north-west from over the Presidio. In the lower foreground, Fort Winfield Scott: rows of barracks, officers' housing along a curving road, parade ground, a wharf running out into the bay at right, bare treeless slopes. At the shore, the twin concrete south pylons and the works at Fort Point. From there the bridge runs away into the frame — the south tower standing on its pier in the water at centre with the catwalk running out to it from shore, then two heavy dark cable curves sweeping across the strait to the far north tower at Lime Point. Behind, the whole sweep of the Marin Headlands, Sausalito and the hills to the horizon under a clouded sky.
details: Construction stage: 19 May 1936, one day before cable spinning was completed. Both towers complete; both main cables visibly spun and hanging in their full curve; the catwalks still in place alongside them; and absolutely no deck — the gap under the cables is open water from tower to tower. The single best 'cables done, deck not started' frame in the pool, and the sharpest file in it.
visible_text: Burned into the lower left: '(0154-32-I-15)(5-19-36-12N)(12-1500)   GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE, CALIF.'
notes: Dated one day before spinning finished on 20 May 1936, ahead of schedule, after 6 months and 9 days. NARA copy 7455640; a mounted archival variant of the same negative also exists on Commons.

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: View from Fort Winfield Scott on the San Francisco side out to the unfinished bridge: the towers standing with the catwalks and spun main cables slung between them, and no roadway.
details: Construction stage: cables spun, deck not yet hung — 1936. Taken from the Army post looking out, so the foreground is military ground rather than the works.
visible_text: None burned into the image; NPS credit line beneath.
notes: Commons title: 'Unfinished Golden Gate Bridge from Fort Scott.'

attribution: U.S. National Park Service / Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Park Archives
depicts: Tall portrait view taken from beside one tower looking along the span. The near tower leg fills the left of the frame as a dark vertical; from it the main cable sweeps down to the right with its cable bands and the vertical suspender ropes already hanging, and the timber catwalk runs away below and parallel to it with derricks and machinery standing on it. Men are visible as small figures along the catwalk. The far tower stands ghostly in haze at upper right; the water and a dark headland fill the bottom right corner.
details: Construction stage: cable spinning / suspender hanging, 1936. There is no deck — the catwalk is the only walking surface, hanging free over the water. The suspender ropes hang straight down into empty air. A reproduction from a printed book, so it is coarse-screened and grainy, but it is the closest view in the pool of the actual spinning operation.
visible_text: Printed caption under the picture: 'Derricks were used to pull the wire over to the San Francisco side.' Credit line beneath: 'Golden Gate NRA, Park Archives, TASC Negative Collection, GOGA 35301.0482'.
notes: Halftone reproduction rather than a photographic print; usable but visibly screened at full size.

attribution: San Francisco Public Library (Flickr Commons)
depicts: Extremely wide, letterbox-shaped photograph of the catwalk being assembled, shot from below and to the side against a blank white sky. A finished section of catwalk runs in from the left, its timber deck and railings supported on a trestle frame, with about seven men standing and working along it. From its end a bare skeletal run of catwalk stringers and cross-slats continues down and away to the right, with two men crawling along it — one halfway, one right at the far end sitting on a small platform. Cable and rope lines cross the sky. Bare hills fill the right background.
details: Construction stage: catwalk erection, before spinning. This is the moment the footbridge is being pushed out over open water: the near end is a finished walkway and the far end is a naked ladder of steel with men on it and nothing underneath. No deck, no cable. Aspect ratio is roughly 2.6:1 (1024x396) — a letterbox strip, so it will need full-bleed banding or a pan, not a normal 16:9 fill.
visible_text: None visible in the image.
notes: San Francisco Public Library title: 'Workmen putting catwalk construction of Golden Gate Bridge into place, San Francisco.' The SFPL Flickr Commons scans are mostly 400 px; this is one of only two in that set large enough to use.

attribution: San Francisco Public Library (Flickr Commons)
depicts: Portrait photograph with a white deckle border. A man in a leather jacket, work trousers, canvas shoes and a metal hard hat stands on a bare timber platform high on a bridge tower, playing a trombone out over the strait, slide extended. Behind and below him is a huge drop to the water and then the whole sweep of the Marin Headlands with a road cutting across them; a riveted tower leg with a diagonal ladder runs up the left edge of the frame, and steel cables run out from the platform. Two oil drums and coils of rope sit on the platform beside him; another workman's head and shoulders show below the platform edge at lower left.
details: Construction stage: tower work, 1936 — the man is standing on a working platform on a completed tower with the main cables already run. The hard hat is worth pointing at: hard hats were a novelty on this job. Portrait format (760x1024).
visible_text: None burned into the image; the print's white border is included.
notes: San Francisco Public Library title: 'Jess Stafford playing his trombone on the Golden Gate Bridge Towers during construction.' Overlaps the labor theme but is included here for the tower-top vantage.

attribution: U.S. Navy
depicts: High aerial looking down on the bridge from the bay side, with the deck under construction. The near (south) tower stands at the right of the frame with the main cable sweeping away left in a long curve, the vertical suspender ropes hanging from it in an even comb, and the roadway steel already hung along most of the span as a narrow open lattice with derricks standing on it. Below and beyond, six or more U.S. Navy warships are strung out in line steaming in through the Golden Gate, the leading three being aircraft carriers with their broad flight decks; Alcatraz sits in the bay at the top of the frame.
details: Construction stage: deck erection, 12 November 1936. The cables are complete, the suspenders are hung, and the floor system has been built out from the towers so that most of the span carries a skeletal deck with erection derricks working on it — but the deck is still open steel, unpaved, and there are visible gaps. The fleet passing underneath gives the clearance a scale.
visible_text: No text burned into the image.
notes: Commons description identifies the carriers, front to rear, as USS Lexington (CV-2), USS Ranger (CV-4) and USS Saratoga (CV-3). Almost the only deck-erection frame in the pool.

attribution: Historic American Engineering Record (HAER), U.S. National Park Service (colour transparency)
depicts: Colour photograph, taken from the Marin vista point garden. In the centre foreground, mounted on a concrete plinth on the path, is a short cut section of one of the bridge's main cables painted international orange, its sawn end facing the camera as a dense grey disc packed with thousands of wire ends, with the cable band bolts standing proud along the top. A white sign board rises behind it. Beyond, over flower beds and clipped shrubs, the completed orange bridge runs away with both towers, cables and deck, the city and hills behind, under a blue sky with cloud.
details: Construction stage: none — this is the completed bridge, photographed decades later, but the cut cable section is the clearest possible illustration of what cable spinning produced: 27,572 individual parallel wires compacted into one 36-inch cable. The sawn face reads as a solid speckled disc at this scale. The sign board carries the cable statistics as printed text.
visible_text: The sign board reads: 'GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE / MAIN SPAN 4200 FT.' with a table beneath — 'LENGTH OF ONE CABLE 7650 ft (2331.7 m)', 'DIAMETER OF CABLE 36 3/8 in (92.4 cm)', 'WIRES IN EACH CABLE 27,572', 'TOTAL WIRE USED 80,000 miles (128,748 km)', 'WEIGHT OF CABLE 24,500 tons (22,226 metric tons)'. A 'DO NOT ENTER / WRONG WAY' road sign is visible at far left. Film rebate along the frame edge reads 'KODAK' and 'HAER NO. CA-31'.
notes: The numbers on the sign match the research figures exactly. A black-and-white version of the same subject exists in the same HAER set; this colour one is the better of the two.

attribution: Historic American Engineering Record (HAER), U.S. National Park Service
depicts: Large-format black and white photograph taken standing on top of the south tower, looking along its axis. The domed steel cable saddle fills the centre of the frame — a big ribbed casting with radiating stiffeners — with the main cable entering it from left and right as two fat pipes wrapped in bands. A steel maintenance stair and ladder run up the middle to a small mast carrying an aircraft warning light. Beyond and far below, the bay on the left and the city of San Francisco on the right; a boat wake in the water at bottom left gives the height.
details: Construction stage: none — completed structure, documented in 1984. Included because it shows the cable seat at the top of the tower, the exact point over which the spinning wheels ran and where the cable's whole load is transferred into the 746 ft tower. The riveted plate construction is clearly visible.
visible_text: Handwritten on the film rebate at the right edge: 'HAER NO. CA-31-31'.
notes: Useful as a detail cutaway when narrating the tower and cable geometry.

attribution: Historic American Engineering Record (HAER), U.S. National Park Service
depicts: Black and white photograph looking up at a section of main cable against a plain grey sky. The cable runs diagonally across the frame as a smooth wrapped cylinder; at its centre a cable band clamps around it, its two halves drawn together by two rows of large bolts standing out like teeth. From the band, four wire suspender ropes drop away downward, gathered by clamps just below the band. A thin handrail cable crosses the sky behind.
details: Construction stage: none — completed structure, 1984 documentation. This is the connection detail that the whole deck hangs from: cable band bolted round the spun cable, suspender ropes looped over it. Very clean, isolated against empty sky, which makes it easy to read as a diagram.
visible_text: Handwritten on the film rebate at the upper left: 'HAER NO. CA-31-15'.
notes: Pairs with construction-47 and construction-48 as a three-image explanation of how the cable works.

attribution: Centpacrr (English Wikipedia)
depicts: Studio photograph of a single original Golden Gate Bridge rivet lying on a plain white background, lit to cast a soft shadow. The domed head at left is coated in weathered international orange paint; the shaft is bare grey steel with bright tool marks, and the far end has been sheared or split so that the metal is peeled back in curled petals.
details: Construction stage: an artefact rather than a scene — a rivet removed from the bridge, shown at large scale against white. Directly illustrates the riveting statistics: the towers were assembled with hundreds of thousands of hand-driven rivets like this. The orange paint on the head and bare steel on the shaft shows how the rivet sat in the structure.
visible_text: No text in the image.
notes: Commons description: 'Original rivet from the Golden Gate Bridge... put together with more than 1.2 million hand installed rivets like this one during its construction which started in January, 1933. The shaft of each rivet measured 1 inch in diameter and the head 1.5 inches.' Note this is the only non-public-domain item in the set: CC BY-SA 3.0, so it needs the attribution shown.
